questions.q: What separates authentication from authorization?
options: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do
Authentication happens on the client; authorization on the server
Authentication uses tokens; authorization uses passwords
Authentication is optional; authorization is legally required

questions.q: Where does session state live in classic cookie-based session auth?
options: Inside the cookie itself, signed but readable by the browser
In the browser's localStorage, keyed by the domain
Replicated across CDN edge nodes located nearest to each individual user
Server-side (store or DB), with the cookie holding only an opaque session ID

questions.q: What makes a JWT verifiable without a database lookup?
options: The token is encrypted, so possession alone proves validity
Every JWT is mirrored into a distributed cache that all services share and consult
Its signature verifies against the issuer's key; the claims are self-contained
The browser validates it against the certificate authority

questions.q: In OAuth 2.0, what is the fundamental role of an access token?
options: It proves the user's password was entered correctly within the last hour
It grants the bearer scoped permission to call protected resources
It encrypts API payloads end to end between client and server
It identifies the client application's developer account

questions.q: Why do OAuth flows issue short-lived access tokens plus a refresh token?
options: Shorter-lived tokens compress far better inside HTTP authorization headers
Refresh tokens let resource servers skip expensive signature checks
Two tokens double the entropy an attacker must guess
A stolen access token expires quickly; the refresh token can be guarded and revoked

questions.q: What does RBAC grant permissions to?
options: Roles that users are assigned, rather than users directly
Each individual user directly, through a per-user access-control list
Resources, which advertise the users they accept
Network segments, delegating checks to the firewall

questions.q: Which flow is recommended for a browser SPA using OAuth 2.0 today?
options: Implicit flow, returning tokens directly in the URL fragment
Authorization code flow with PKCE
Resource owner password flow with the user's credentials
Client credentials flow using a secret embedded in the JS bundle

questions.q: Why must passwords be hashed with an intentionally slow algorithm (bcrypt, argon2) rather than fast SHA-256?
options: Slow hashing algorithms produce longer digests that databases can index more efficiently
SHA-256 is reversible when given enough examples
Slowness throttles offline brute-force attempts against a stolen hash database
Fast hashes expire and must be recomputed monthly

questions.q: A microservice fleet must check 'is this request allowed?' on every call. Why do teams often pick JWTs here?
options: JWTs are essentially immune to theft, unlike opaque session identifiers stored in cookies
Each service verifies tokens locally with the public key, skipping a central auth call
JWTs rotate automatically on every request hop
Opaque tokens cannot cross service boundaries at all

questions.q: The security team must lock out a compromised account immediately. Why are stateless JWTs a problem?
options: JWT claims are encrypted by default, so the compromised account ID cannot even be read
Signature verification is already too slow to add a blocklist check on top
Issued tokens stay valid until expiry unless you add revocation state back in
JWTs cannot carry an expiry claim, so they never lapse

questions.q: Where should a refresh token for a web app be stored to reduce XSS risk?
options: In an HttpOnly, Secure cookie inaccessible to page JavaScript
In localStorage, so it survives tab closes
Inside a global JavaScript variable that gets renewed on every full page load
In the URL query string, so it travels with navigation

questions.q: 'Managers may edit reports of their own department during business hours.' Which model expresses this naturally?
options: RBAC with one role per department-hour combination
An ACL entry per report, updated by a nightly job
OAuth scopes granted per department and refreshed at the top of every business hour
ABAC, evaluating user, resource, and environment attributes per request

questions.q: Why does OAuth's authorization code flow return a code first instead of tokens directly?
options: Authorization codes are much shorter strings, fitting within strict browser URL length limits
The code doubles as a CSRF token for the login form
Tokens are fetched server-to-server, keeping them out of browser history and referrers
Codes allow the user to approve each API call individually

questions.q: What attack does the state parameter in OAuth flows prevent?
options: Replay of expired access tokens against the resource server
CSRF: an attacker binding their authorization response to the victim's session
Brute-forcing of the client secret via timing
A protocol downgrade from PKCE-protected code flow to the legacy implicit flow

questions.q: A user's permissions changed, but their JWT still carries the old role claim for 15 more minutes. Standard mitigation?
options: Sign all tokens with a continuously rotating key so older claims fail verification
Have every service re-derive roles from the username string
Push new JWTs to all logged-in devices over WebSockets
Keep token lifetimes short and re-check critical permissions server-side

questions.q: Why is 'the user is logged in' insufficient as an authorization check for GET /invoices/123?
options: Ownership must be verified, or any user can read others' invoices by changing the ID
Financial documents such as invoices always require a second authentication factor by standard
GET requests bypass authorization in most frameworks
The check fails for users with multiple sessions

questions.q: Refresh token rotation with reuse detection: what does the server do when a rotated-out (old) refresh token is presented?
options: Honors it once more, then retires it permanently
Issues one new access token but quietly flags the account for later manual review
Extends the old token's life to avoid breaking the client
Treats it as theft evidence and revokes the entire token family

questions.q: An API gateway validates JWTs; internal services then trust the gateway's identity headers. What deployment mistake breaks this model?
options: Allowing direct network reach to internal services, letting anyone forge the identity headers
Rotating the JWT signing keys more than once per day
Using RS256 signatures instead of HS256 at the gateway
Caching validated tokens at the gateway for their lifetime

questions.q: Sessions in Redis: what failure mode do you accept versus stateless JWTs?
options: Session IDs become guessable as the store fills up
Every user must re-authenticate on each application deploy regardless of store health
An auth-store outage can block all logins and permission checks fleet-wide
CSRF protection stops working without token claims

questions.q: Zero-trust internal architecture: which statement captures the auth implication?
options: Perimeter TLS suffices; internal calls can stay anonymous for speed
Every service-to-service call is authenticated and authorized, e.g., via mTLS plus policy
Internal traffic needs authorization only when it crosses regions
A shared static API key per environment satisfies zero trust
